lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: The lamp on Cael's bench was lying, and it was doing it beautifully.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: A courier had brought it in that morning wrapped in a shirt, the way people brought things they were embarrassed to be attached to. It was a good lamp — Concern-made, the brass turned on a proper lathe, the lumen-cell seated square. By every rule she had ever been taught it should have thrown a clean, cold light for another twenty years. Instead it guttered, brightened, guttered, like a person trying to remember a name.

lines.speaker: Cael Ferren
lines.text: "You flicker in company,"

lines.speaker: Cael Ferren
lines.text: "and you're steady when you're alone. So it isn't the cell."

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: She said it out loud because the shop was empty and because saying a fault out loud was half of finding it. Her father had done the same, at this same bench, for thirty years, and the habit had outlived him the way the salt smell of the harbor outlived the tide. His stool still stood by the window. She had not moved it. She had not sat on it either.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: The trade way to fix a lying lamp was to swap the cell, bill for the cell, and send it home. Any brass-rank artificer in Threnn could do it blind. Cael turned the lamp over, thumbed the sigil-plate open, and did not swap the cell, because she already knew the cell was fine. She knew it the way she knew the weather was about to turn — a pressure under the back teeth, a note just below hearing.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: That was the part she never billed for. The part she never mentioned.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: She took the resonance fork down from its nail. It was an ugly thing, older than the shop, two tines of grey steel on a stub of horn, and it had been her one true inheritance in the sense that no one else had wanted it. She held it a hand's breadth from the lamp and did not strike it.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: It rang anyway. Faint, and wrong, a note that leaned.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: Cael let out a breath she'd been holding since the courier left. There it was. The lamp wasn't broken. It was tuned — tuned to a note that wasn't in the room, a note from somewhere the fork could hear and she was not supposed to be able to. A lamp built to sit still in the ordinary Facet, quietly listening for a deeper one, and flinching every time it caught the edge of it.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: Somebody had made this lamp sensitive on purpose. Or something near where it had been made had leaked.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: She wrapped the fork in a cloth before its ringing could settle into her jaw, and she stood for a moment with both hands flat on the cool brass, feeling the flicker come and go under her palms like a pulse. If she took it to the Schools they would call her a liar. If she took it to the Wardens they would take the lamp, and then they would take a closer look at the woman who had known, at a glance, what a lamp was listening to.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: So she did what she always did. She swapped the cell it didn't need, so the bill would make sense. She filed the sigil-plate a hair to deafen it, so it would stop flinching in company. She wrote cell fatigue — replaced on the ticket, in the careful hand of a woman who could not afford to be interesting, and she set the lamp on the shelf for collection, steady now, and honest, and a little less than it had been.

lines.speaker: Cael Ferren
lines.text: "There,"

lines.speaker: Cael Ferren
lines.text: "Now you'll get on."

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: The lamp threw a clean cold light and told no one anything, which was, Cael had decided a long time ago, the only safe way to be made.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: The Commission Hall smelled of chalk and wet wool and the particular ambition of people waiting to be chosen. Cael found her Company where she always found them: under the slate board, arguing.

lines.speaker: Iven Sarraz
lines.text: "It is not a matter of pride,"

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: Iven was saying, in the voice he used when it was entirely a matter of pride.

lines.speaker: Iven Sarraz
lines.text: "It is a matter of category. Manufactory Nine is a structural clearance. That is brass work. We are — arguably — silver."

lines.speaker: Brick Halvorn
lines.text: "We're brass,"

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: Brick said, comfortably, without looking up from the apple he was quartering with a knife the length of Cael's forearm.

lines.speaker: Brick Halvorn
lines.text: "Board says brass. We eat brass wages. That makes us brass."

lines.speaker: Iven Sarraz
lines.text: "We are capable of silver."

lines.speaker: Brick Halvorn
lines.text: "So's a lot of folk. Board doesn't rank what you can do. Ranks what you've done."

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: Nettle was sitting on the board's frame itself, six feet up, where no one had seen her climb.

lines.speaker: Nettle
lines.text: "The Nine pays double,"

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: she said, to the room in general.

lines.speaker: Nettle
lines.text: "It's been on the slate eleven weeks and nobody's taken it. That's not a brass job that pays double. That's a job somebody wants gone."

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: Cael read the chalk. Manufactory Nine, Ash District. Structural survey & clearance. Lumen Concern, sealed. Rank: brass. Fee: 2×. She did not like the seal. A Concern seal on a clearance meant the Concern wanted a receipt more than it wanted the work — wanted to be able to say, later, to someone, that a licensed party had gone in and found nothing.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: Under the back teeth, faint, the pressure turned.

lines.speaker: Haldane Threll
lines.text: "Ferren."

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: Haldane Threll had come down the length of the Hall without seeming to cross it, which was a trick of hers Cael had never worked out. Mistress of Commissions, grey-coated, a face like a closed ledger.

lines.speaker: Haldane Threll
lines.text: "Your Company's short a job this month."

lines.speaker: Brick Halvorn
lines.text: "We're choosy,"

lines.speaker: Haldane Threll
lines.text: "You're broke,"

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: said Threll, not unkindly.

lines.speaker: Haldane Threll
lines.text: "The Nine wants a party by week's end. It's straightforward. Concern lost the building nine years ago to a collapse; they've finally decided to clear the lot and sell the ground. Someone reputable walks it, certifies it empty and safe, signs the token, collects double."

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: She looked at Cael when she said reputable, which Cael tried not to read anything into and read everything into anyway.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: Across the Hall, two people were not queuing. A Concern clerk in a good coat, watching the board without appearing to. And by the door, grey on grey, hands folded, a Warden — not looking at anyone, which was how you knew a Warden was looking at everyone.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: Cael's mouth had gone dry.

lines.speaker: Cael Ferren
lines.text: "Why's it still on the board at eleven weeks if it's straightforward?"

lines.speaker: Haldane Threll
lines.text: "Because it's dull and it's in the Ash District and it pays in Concern scrip until certification,"

lines.speaker: Haldane Threll
lines.text: "Parties want glory or coin up front. You want neither. You want a clean job and to be left alone. I have read you correctly for six years, Ferren; do not disappoint me by developing standards now."

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: Iven opened his mouth, presumably to reclassify something. Brick got there first.

lines.speaker: Brick Halvorn
lines.text: "We'll take it,"

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: he said, and quartered the last of the apple, and handed Cael the seedless middle, which was the piece she liked, which he had never once mentioned knowing.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: Threll produced the commission-token — a brass chit, warm from her pocket, the Concern seal biting one face and the Hall's biting the other. She set it in Cael's palm.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: It hummed. Low, and level, and wrong, exactly the note the lamp had leaned toward all morning. Cael closed her hand around it before her face could do anything, and smiled the small careful smile of a woman collecting a dull job, and did not look at the Warden by the door.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: Nettle walked her home, which meant Nettle appeared beside her on Kettle Lane without having been there a moment before, matching her stride as if she'd been there the whole time.

lines.speaker: Nettle
lines.text: "You went white,"

lines.speaker: Nettle
lines.text: "At the board. When Threll gave you the token."

lines.speaker: Cael Ferren
lines.text: "It's cold in the Hall."

lines.speaker: Nettle
lines.text: "It's the warmest room in the district. They vent the lumen furnace under the floor."

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: Nettle wasn't looking at her. Nettle was looking at the lamps coming up along the lane as the light went, one after another, a soft cold blue blooming down toward the harbor.

lines.speaker: Nettle
lines.text: "You do that. Go somewhere behind your eyes. I've watched you do it over a busted lock and a full purse. I never worked out what you're listening for."

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: Cael turned the token over in her pocket. It had not stopped humming. It would not stop humming until she was well away from it, and she could not be well away from it, because it was the seal on a job that would feed the four of them through the winter.

lines.speaker: Cael Ferren
lines.text: "Can I ask you something,"

lines.speaker: Cael Ferren
lines.text: "and you don't make it a thing."

lines.speaker: Nettle
lines.text: "My favorite kind of question."

lines.speaker: Cael Ferren
lines.text: "The gaps you cross. The ones on the roofs, the one over the Cutwater last spring — six feet of open air, and you were on the far side of it before you jumped."

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: Nettle's stride hitched, very slightly, the first ungraceful thing Cael had ever seen her do.

lines.speaker: Nettle
lines.text: "Luck,"

lines.speaker: Nettle
lines.text: "Good feet. My gran's bead."

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: She touched the river-worn charm at her throat, a habit so old she plainly didn't know she was doing it.

lines.speaker: Nettle
lines.text: "Why."

lines.speaker: Cael Ferren
lines.text: "No reason. Long day."

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: Because you and I are the same, Cael did not say. Because whatever you feel when you cross a gap that isn't there, I feel when I put my hand on a lamp that's listening to something under the world, and neither of us is supposed to be able to, and one of us has learned to hide it and the other hasn't noticed she has anything to hide.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: They walked. The token hummed against her hip. Somewhere behind them, a soft cold blue lamp caught the edge of it and guttered, once, and steadied, and told no one anything.

lines.speaker: Nettle
lines.text: "Ash District tomorrow,"

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: Nettle said, at the door of the glimmerworks, and grinned, and was gone before Cael's key was in the lock — not vanished, nothing so grand, just around a corner faster than a person could go, into a gap in the evening that closed behind her like water.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: The Ash District had been the bright edge of Threnn once, back when the Concern's manufactories ran day and night and the whole quarter glowed like a banked fire. Now the lumen-lamps along the Nine Road stood at long intervals, half of them dark, and the light between them was the ordinary grey of a city that had stopped paying attention.

lines.speaker: Iven Sarraz
lines.text: "The lamps thin out the closer we get,"

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: Iven noted. He had his coat collar up and his School manner on, which meant he was uneasy and disguising it as observation.

lines.speaker: Iven Sarraz
lines.text: "Someone's stopped maintaining the line."

lines.speaker: Brick Halvorn
lines.text: "Someone's stopped everything,"

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: Brick said. Gudgeon rode his shoulder, the great enchanted head of the maul wrapped in sacking so it wouldn't catch the light and worry people.

lines.speaker: Brick Halvorn
lines.text: "Nine years. You'd think the Concern would've cleared its own lot sooner."

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: At the last inhabited corner an old road-warden sat outside a watch-hut, not the grey-cloaked kind but the ordinary kind, a pensioner with a lantern and a ledger of who came and went. Old Sedge, the plate on the hut said, though the man didn't offer his name and Cael didn't ask. He looked at the commission-token Brick showed him, and he looked at the four of them a good while longer.
"You're for the Nine,"

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: Sedge said. It wasn't a question.
"Concern's fourth party."

lines.speaker: Iven Sarraz
lines.text: "Board said we were the first,"
"Board says a lot."

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: Sedge spat, precisely, into the gutter.
"Three went in before you, over the years. Signed my ledger going. None of 'em signed it coming out that I saw, and I see everything comes down this road. Maybe they left another way."

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: He did not sound like a man who believed there was another way.
"You'll want to be out before the light's full gone. Place doesn't like the dark. Or it likes it too much. I never worked out which."

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: Nettle had drifted ahead while he talked, the way she did, and now she was standing at the mouth of the yard where the Nine's broken silhouette blocked the last of the sky — standing there, and then she wasn't, and then she was ten feet further on, on the far side of a fallen gate that a person would have had to climb.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: She looked back, startled, as if her own feet had surprised her. Her hand had gone to the bead at her throat.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: Under Cael's back teeth the pressure turned, and turned, and did not stop turning. The fork in her satchel — wrapped, deafened, silent for a decade — gave a single, muffled ring, like a struck note heard through a wall.

lines.speaker: Iven Sarraz
lines.text: "Cael?"

lines.speaker: Iven Sarraz
lines.text: "You've gone the color of the road."

lines.speaker: Cael Ferren
lines.text: "I'm fine."

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: She made herself walk toward the gate, toward Nettle, toward the dark bulk of the thing the Concern wanted certified empty.

lines.speaker: Cael Ferren
lines.text: "Let's get it done and get out. Sedge is right about the light."

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: The door of Manufactory Nine was an ordinary door in an ordinary wall of soot-black brick, and it opened onto a room that could not have fit inside the building.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: Brick went first, because that was what Brick was for, Gudgeon unwrapped now and throwing back the light of Iven's summoned flame in dull red flakes. He took three steps and stopped so suddenly that Nettle walked into his back.

lines.speaker: Brick Halvorn
lines.text: "That's not right,"

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: he said, slowly.

lines.speaker: Brick Halvorn
lines.text: "Cael. Come look and tell me why that's not right, because I can't."

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: The manufactory floor ran away from them further than the building was wide. Cael had stood in the yard; she had paced the outer wall while Iven fussed the door-sigil; she knew to the yard how big the Nine was. And the room in front of her was bigger than the yard. Ranks of dead glimmer-looms marched off into a dark that had a horizon. Off to the left a stair went up to a gallery that, by the geometry of the outside, would have to be standing in the street.

lines.speaker: Iven Sarraz
lines.text: "It's folded,"

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: Iven said. His School voice had gone very quiet.

lines.speaker: Iven Sarraz
lines.text: "I've read of it. I never — it's a Fold. Space, bent back on itself. The inside is larger than the out because the inside doesn't agree with the out."

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: He laughed, once, without humor.

lines.speaker: Iven Sarraz
lines.text: "This is not a structural clearance. Threll sent us to certify a deep-Facet wound as an empty warehouse."

lines.speaker: Brick Halvorn
lines.text: "Wardens' work,"

lines.speaker: Brick Halvorn
lines.text: "That's Wardens' work, that is. We should turn round."

lines.speaker: Nettle
lines.text: "The token's Concern-sealed,"

lines.speaker: Nettle
lines.text: "We turn round, we don't get paid, and the Concern gets to say a party went in and lost its nerve. And they send a fourth."

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: She hadn't moved from the doorway. She was gripping the frame.

lines.speaker: Nettle
lines.text: "Or a fifth."

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: Cael barely heard them. She had her hand in her satchel, on the wrapped fork, and through three folds of cloth it was screaming.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: Not ringing. Screaming — a note so high and so wrong it had gone past sound into a pressure that filled her skull and pushed at the backs of her eyes, the small under-the-teeth hum she had managed and hidden and filed down her whole life turned suddenly to a siren she could not deafen. She dragged the fork out. The cloth had scorched brown around it. The grey steel tines were blurred with the speed of their own shaking.

lines.speaker: Iven Sarraz
lines.text: "Cael."

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: Iven was staring at the fork. At her face. Putting things together with the terrible quickness of a clever man who has just realized he has been wrong about a category for years.

lines.speaker: Iven Sarraz
lines.text: "Cael. How did you know the lamp was listening. This morning. How did you know the token hummed."

lines.speaker: Cael Ferren
lines.text: "Later,"

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: Cael said, through her teeth, and the fork screamed, and somewhere out in the folded dark, far off among the dead looms, a single candle was burning that no one had lit.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: They went toward the candle because it was the only light in the folded dark that wasn't theirs, and because Cael's fork pointed at it — the screaming softened by a hair when she aimed the tines that way, like a compass easing when it finds the pole.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: It sat on an overturned crate in a cleared space among the looms, a plain tallow candle burned down to a thumb's width, its flame steady in air that should have had a draft. Beside it lay a knife, a tin cup, a heel of bread gone hard. Someone had made a small camp here. Recently. The bread was days old at most.

lines.speaker: Brick Halvorn
lines.text: "Three parties,"

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: Brick said, quietly.

lines.speaker: Brick Halvorn
lines.text: "Sedge said three went in."

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: Iven crouched by the candle, careful not to touch, his Ward-sense out — Cael could feel it, a cool geometry laid over the air, the one School discipline she'd always half-envied.

lines.speaker: Iven Sarraz
lines.text: "The wax,"

lines.speaker: Iven Sarraz
lines.text: "Watch the wax."

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: They watched. The candle burned. A bead of tallow swelled at the rim, brimmed, and ran down the side — and stopped, and drew back up, and climbed the candle, and sank into the pool at the wick, and the candle was a hair taller than it had been. The flame ate the wax. The wax un-ate itself. The thumb's width of tallow did not shrink.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: Nobody said anything for a moment. Cael became aware that she had stopped breathing.

lines.speaker: Cael Ferren
lines.text: "Do it again,"

lines.speaker: Cael Ferren
lines.text: "Brick. Your hand. The old scratch on the back of your hand, from the gate."

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: Brick turned his hand over. He had caught it on the fallen gate coming in — a shallow red graze across two knuckles, an hour old, already scabbing. As they watched it lifted. The scab lifted and thinned and became a bright bead of blood, and the bead sank back into the skin, and the graze closed to a red line, and the red line paled, and his hand was whole and unmarked as it had been that morning before they ever reached the Nine.

lines.speaker: Iven Sarraz
lines.text: "Hour,"

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: Iven breathed.

lines.speaker: Iven Sarraz
lines.text: "Not just Fold. Hour. The place isn't only bent in space. It's caught in time. It's — running the same stretch, over and over, and pulling everything in it back to the start."

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: He looked up, and for the first time since Cael had known him there was no lecture in his face at all, only a clever man doing sums that frightened him.

lines.speaker: Iven Sarraz
lines.text: "How long a stretch? An hour? A day? How long have we —"

lines.speaker: Nettle
lines.text: "We just walked in,"

lines.speaker: Nettle
lines.text: "We've been in here — what, a quarter hour."

lines.speaker: Iven Sarraz
lines.text: "Have we,"

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: The candle burned. The wax climbed. And out beyond the ring of their light, from the direction Cael's fork had been pointing all along, a voice said, conversationally, out of the folded dark:

lines.speaker: Odeline Marran
lines.text: "You always find the candle first. Every time. I've started leaving it lit for you."

lines.speaker: Iven Sarraz
lines.text: "Don't answer it,"

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: Iven said, low and fast, gripping Cael's sleeve.

lines.speaker: Iven Sarraz
lines.text: "We don't know what it is. We map first. We prove what's happening before we talk to it."

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: It was, Cael thought, the most sensible thing anyone had said since they came in, and it was terrifying that a School mage was the one saying it, because it meant Iven was as far off the edge of what he knew as the rest of them.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: So they mapped. Brick took a nail and scratched a tally into the iron leg of the nearest loom — one stroke — and they walked a slow circuit through the folded dark, past the candle, past a second door that opened onto the same manufactory floor from the wrong side, past a window that looked out on the yard in daylight though it had been dusk when they entered. They came back to the loom. Brick's single tally was gone. The iron was unmarked.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: He scratched it again. Two strokes, this time, and pressed hard, and said

lines.speaker: Brick Halvorn
lines.text: "There. Nobody tell me I miscounted,"

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: and they walked the circuit again, and came back, and the iron was smooth.

lines.speaker: Iven Sarraz
lines.text: "It resets,"

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: Iven said. He had gone somewhere very calm, the calm of a man holding a fact too large to feel yet.

lines.speaker: Iven Sarraz
lines.text: "Matter resets. The candle, Brick's hand, the tally. The Hour pulls everything back to the start of the loop. Everything in it."

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: He looked at his own hands, turning them over.

lines.speaker: Iven Sarraz
lines.text: "But not us. We remember the circuit. We remember the candle. Why do we remember and the iron doesn't?"

lines.speaker: Nettle
lines.text: "Because we're alive,"

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: Nettle said. She had her back to a loom and her charm in her fist.

lines.speaker: Nettle
lines.text: "Or because we came from outside. Or —"

lines.speaker: Nettle
lines.text: "I don't know why I said that. I don't know how I'd know that."

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: Cael did. She was beginning to, anyway, in the place behind her teeth where she had spent her whole life not-knowing things on purpose. The Hour reset the world. It did not reset the people who could feel the deeper Facets, because those people were, in some way she had no word for, standing slightly outside the loom themselves. Nettle, who crossed gaps that weren't there. Herself, who heard what lamps were listening to.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: She set her hand flat on the iron leg where Brick's tally kept vanishing, and she let the fork ring against her palm, and she felt the loop turn under her hand like a great wheel going round — felt where it started, felt where it would drag them back to, felt, faint and terrible, that it had been turning a very, very long time.

lines.speaker: Cael Ferren
lines.text: "It's about an hour,"

lines.speaker: Cael Ferren
lines.text: "The loop. A little under. It starts when someone crosses the threshold, and it ends —"

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: she swallowed

lines.speaker: Cael Ferren
lines.text: "it ends, and starts again, and anyone inside who can't feel it forgets the whole turn and lives it fresh. That's why the parties never came out. They're not dead. They're still walking in. Every hour. For nine years."

lines.speaker: Iven Sarraz
lines.text: "Then how,"

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: said Iven, very quietly

lines.speaker: Iven Sarraz
lines.text: "does the thing at the candle remember us?"

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: She was sitting on the crate by the candle when they came back to it, as if she had been there the whole time, which — Cael was beginning to understand — she had, in every sense the word could bear.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: A woman of middle years, or she wore the face of one; grey coming in at the temples of hair that had been dark, a Concern surveyor's coat gone soft and pale with age, boots mended and re-mended with wire. She had a stopped pocket-watch open in one hand and she was not looking at it. She was looking at Cael, and her eyes were the steadiest thing in the folded dark.

lines.speaker: Odeline Marran
lines.text: "Odeline Marran,"

lines.speaker: Odeline Marran
lines.text: "Ode. Fourth survey, Lumen Concern, the year the Nine came down. You'll be the — "

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: she tilted her head, considering

lines.speaker: Odeline Marran
lines.text: "the fifty-first party, I think, or near it. I stopped keeping the count on the outside years ago. You're the one that matters, though. You've been the one that matters for eleven turns now."

lines.speaker: Brick Halvorn
lines.text: "You know us,"

lines.speaker: Brick Halvorn
lines.text: "You called Cael by — nobody said our names."

lines.speaker: Odeline Marran
lines.text: "You've told me your names sixty times, big man. You just haven't done it yet, this turn."

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: Ode smiled, and it was a kind smile, and the loneliest thing Cael had ever seen.

lines.speaker: Odeline Marran
lines.text: "It's all right. It's a lot. It was a lot for me too, the first hundred hours. You get a shape for it eventually. You have to, or you go the way the third party went, and I'd rather you didn't. There were four of them. They're still in the east gallery. They think it's the day they arrived. It's kinder not to visit."

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: She held up the watch. Its hands stood at seven minutes past some hour, frozen, and around the frozen hands the whole ruin turned.

lines.speaker: Odeline Marran
lines.text: "It stopped when the loop caught,"

lines.speaker: Odeline Marran
lines.text: "Seven past. It starts here, it ends at the top of the hour, it comes back to seven past. I've had a long time to learn the shape of one hour, artificer. A long time. And in all of it you are the first person to walk in through that door already able to hear it."

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: She looked at Cael's fork, still shivering in her hand.

lines.speaker: Odeline Marran
lines.text: "You've been hiding that your whole life, haven't you. Don't. Not in here. In here it's the only thing that's going to get any of us out."

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: Cael's throat had closed. Behind her she could feel the others go still — Iven, who had guessed; Brick, who was catching up; Nettle, who had gone white, because Nettle was hearing, for the first time, someone say out loud the thing Nettle had never let herself think about the gaps she crossed.

lines.speaker: Cael Ferren
lines.text: "Get us out how,"

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: Cael managed.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: Ode closed the watch.

lines.speaker: Odeline Marran
lines.text: "That's the long part,"

lines.speaker: Odeline Marran
lines.text: "Sit down. We have exactly as much time as we've always had, and we've always had enough, if we're quick. Let me tell you what the Nine was really making, before it fell."

lines.speaker: Odeline Marran
lines.text: "You were taught the Facets like a ladder,"

lines.speaker: Odeline Marran
lines.text: "Brass artifice at the bottom. The Schools in the middle. And at the top, if your teachers were honest, which mine weren't, the deep two — Fold and Hour, space and time, that the Wardens bury and don't let anyone climb to. A ladder. Rungs. Separate things, and you pick one and you stay on it."

lines.speaker: Iven Sarraz
lines.text: "That's the law,"

lines.speaker: Iven Sarraz
lines.text: "That's — that's the first thing they teach. The Facets are distinct disciplines. You can't cross them."

lines.speaker: Odeline Marran
lines.text: "You can't cross them now,"

lines.speaker: Odeline Marran
lines.text: "Because someone took an axe to something that was never a ladder. It was a wheel. One art, whole, turning — and it was broken, on purpose, a long time before Threnn, and the pieces were tiered and taught as separate so that only the safe, small piece, the artifice, would ever be common. So no one would ever again hold the Whole."

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: She said it without drama, the way you'd describe a wall.

lines.speaker: Odeline Marran
lines.text: "The histories in the Cloister call it the Sundering. The Concern didn't know that word. The Concern just knew that here, in the Ash District, the ground remembered being unbroken, and if you built a manufactory over that spot and dug a lumen-well deep enough, you could tap it. A place where the Facets bleed back into each other. Where a shard of the Whole still sits in the rock like a splinter in a thumb."

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: She stood, and walked to the edge of the candle-light, and the others followed because there was nothing else to do, and she pointed down through a broken grate in the manufactory floor into a shaft that went further than the fork could hear the bottom of.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: Down there, faint, was a light that was every color the eye could hold and one it couldn't.

lines.speaker: Odeline Marran
lines.text: "The Keystone,"

lines.speaker: Odeline Marran
lines.text: "The Concern dug for lumen and struck the Whole. It started bleeding. Space folded. Time caught. The building came down in the first turn of the loop and it's been coming down every turn since, and I've been standing here for nine years of hours trying to work out how to reach a thing that resets itself to the bottom of a shaft every time I get close."

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: She turned to Cael.

lines.speaker: Odeline Marran
lines.text: "And now a woman walks in who can hear exactly where the note is. So. Artificer. That splinter is un-breaking the world one folded room at a time, and it has all the time there has ever been to do it in. What do you say we go down there and decide whether to pull it out."

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: The fork in Cael's hand had stopped screaming. Pointed down the shaft, at the Keystone, at the un-shattering heart of everything she had spent her life pretending she couldn't feel, it had gone perfectly, terribly still — a struck note, held, resolving at last into the thing it had always been reaching for.

lines.speaker: Cael Ferren
lines.text: "That note,"

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: Cael said, unsteadily.

lines.speaker: Cael Ferren
lines.text: "The one I've heard under everything since I was a girl. That's it. That's what I've been hearing. It's been calling the whole time."

lines.speaker: Odeline Marran
lines.text: "Yes,"

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: said Ode, gently.

lines.speaker: Odeline Marran
lines.text: "It calls all of us who can hear it. It called me down a road in the Ash District nine years ago."

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: She put her old, wire-mended hand on Cael's shoulder.

lines.speaker: Odeline Marran
lines.text: "The trick, and I say this as the one person alive who knows — the trick is deciding whether to answer. Now. Before the hour turns. I'll want to know about the Gattick line while we walk — whether the Concern ever ran the second shaft they were surveying when I — well. Later. Come down. Bring the flame. And whatever you do, don't let the mage touch it first; he'll want to understand it, and this isn't a thing you get to understand before you decide."

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: Reaching the Keystone was a problem with four moving parts and less than an hour to solve it in, and — Ode pointed out, briskly, as they worked — they had solved it eleven times already; they simply couldn't remember, because the last eleven times the hour had turned before they got out, and reset everyone who couldn't hold the deep Facets back to the top of the stairs.

lines.speaker: Odeline Marran
lines.text: "So we do it fast,"

lines.speaker: Odeline Marran
lines.text: "and we do it in the right order, and this time the person carrying it is one of the ones the loop can't reset. That's you, artificer. That's the change. That's why this is the turn that matters."

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: They worked it like a job, because a job was the one thing the Kettle-Iron Company knew how to do. Nettle went first — down the shaft in a series of blinks, gaps that shouldn't be there and were, her charm blazing at her throat, Ode calling the timing because Ode had watched the shaft fold and unfold a thousand times and knew to the breath when each drop would hold. Brick anchored the rope Nettle couldn't carry, Gudgeon wedged across the grate, taking a weight that would have pulled a lesser tool through the floor. Iven laid a Ward across the bottom of the shaft — not to hold the Keystone, he'd finally understood, but to hold the time steady in one small bubble, a School discipline bent to a purpose no School would sanction, sweat standing on his face as he held a second still against an hour that wanted to turn.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: And Cael went down into the light.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: Up close the Keystone was small — a shard the size of a thumb, exactly as Ode had said, and it did not look like the engine of anything. It looked like a chip of grey rock with a crack of impossible color running through it, and it sat in the raw stone of the shaft-bottom humming the note she had heard under lamps and locks and the whole of her hidden life, and when she reached for it every instinct she'd built for twenty-six years told her to pull her hand back, to file it down, to write cell fatigue — replaced and walk away and be a little less than she was so that no one would ever look too closely.

lines.speaker: Iven Sarraz
lines.text: "Now, Cael,"

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: Iven's voice came down the shaft, cracking with strain.

lines.speaker: Iven Sarraz
lines.text: "I cannot hold the hour much — now —"

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: She stopped hiding. For the first time in her life, on purpose, wide open, she let the deep Facet fill her hand the way it had always wanted to — and the note answered, and the crack of color leaned toward her like a plant toward light, and she closed her fingers around the shard of the Whole and it came out of the stone as easily as a splinter from a thumb.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: The humming stopped. Every sound in the Nine stopped. And in the enormous ringing silence, up at the top of the shaft, a great many boots came through the door at once.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: They came in from both ends of the folded floor at the same moment, which — Cael would think later — was the only fair thing about it: the two powers that had circled the Nine for nine years, arriving to find the one turn of the hour in which someone had actually pulled the splinter out.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: From the yard door, Concern men in good coats, and behind them Consul Auberon Vasht himself, who had not walked into the Ash District in a decade and had walked in tonight because his instruments had finally gone quiet.

lines.speaker: Auberon Vasht
lines.text: "You have it,"

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: he said, looking at Cael's closed fist with a hunger he didn't trouble to hide.

lines.speaker: Auberon Vasht
lines.text: "Careful, artificer. You are holding the single most valuable object in Threnn, and you have no idea how to keep it working. I do. Name your fee. The Concern is generous to reasonable people."

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: From the far door, grey on grey, no boots at all where there should have been boots: Warden Ophra Kell, alone, hands folded, exactly as she had stood by the Hall door two days and a thousand hours ago. She did not look at the Keystone. She looked at Cael.

lines.speaker: Ophra Kell
lines.text: "It doesn't work,"

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: Kell said, to Vasht, without heat.

lines.speaker: Ophra Kell
lines.text: "It bleeds. It has been bleeding for nine years and it took nine years of a good surveyor's life"

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: a small nod to Ode

lines.speaker: Ophra Kell
lines.text: "and three parties besides. It is not an asset, Consul. It is a wound. The Order will take it to the Cloister and it will be buried where it can bleed into nothing, as the Sundering intended."

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: And then, to Cael, in the same even voice, the thing Cael had spent her whole life crossing streets to avoid:

lines.speaker: Ophra Kell
lines.text: "You pulled it out with your bare hand. Do you know how few living people could do that? I have been looking for you since you were a lamp-mender who knew too much. Give me the shard, and come to the Cloister, and let us make you safe."

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: Safe. The Warden word for buried.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: Ode's hand found Cael's free one and gripped it, hard.

lines.speaker: Odeline Marran
lines.text: "The hour's turning,"

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: Ode murmured, under the two of them, under all of it.

lines.speaker: Odeline Marran
lines.text: "Six minutes. When it turns, everyone in here who can't hold the deep goes back to the stairs and forgets — Vasht, his men, all of them. But not you. Not me. Not the mage while he holds his Ward, and not the scout while she holds her charm. In six minutes this room empties itself of every person who wants to take that thing from you, and you will be standing here holding it and free to walk out the door with the whole of your life in your fist."

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: She squeezed.

lines.speaker: Odeline Marran
lines.text: "Or hand it to the Consul, or the Warden, and be paid, or be safe, and let it go on bleeding, or let it go on buried. You have six minutes and one turn of the hour to decide, and you are the first person in nine years who gets to."

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: Vasht was still talking. Kell was still watching. The candle, somewhere behind them, burned and un-burned. And Cael Ferren, brass rank, lamp-mender, who had never once in her life let anyone see what she could do, opened her hand a crack and looked at the impossible color and felt the whole broken wheel of the world lean toward her, waiting to be answered.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: The hour turned.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: It turned the way Ode had said it would — a great soft wheeling, felt more than heard, and between one breath and the next the folded floor was empty of Concern men. Vasht was gone mid-word, reset to the threshold, walking in again somewhere behind them already forgetting he had ever reached the candle. Warden Kell was gone. The looms stood dead and dark. The candle, on its crate, burned a thumb's width tall.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: Five of them stood in the ringing quiet: an artificer, a mage grey-faced and swaying from a Ward held too long, a front-liner with a maul, a scout with her fist locked round a river-worn bead, and a surveyor who had waited nine years of hours for exactly this and could not quite believe it had come.

lines.speaker: Cael Ferren
lines.text: "Out,"

lines.speaker: Cael Ferren
lines.text: "Now. While the door remembers being a door."

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: They went out the way they'd come in, and this time the room let them, and the ordinary door of Manufactory Nine opened onto the ordinary yard, and the dusk was exactly the dusk they had left — no time passed at all on the outside, because inside there had only ever been the one hour, turning. Old Sedge was in his hut. He looked up, and counted them, and Cael watched him count five where four had gone in, and watched him decide, in the way of a man who saw everything and reported little, to say nothing about it.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: Ode stood in the yard with her face turned up to a sky she hadn't seen change in nine years, and wept without any sound, and Brick put his coat around her shoulders without a word.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: Cael's fist was still closed. She could feel the Keystone through her fingers, the note gone quiet now that she held it, the crack of color waiting. Vasht would come for it; the Concern did not forget a wound it wanted to sell. Kell would come for it, and for her; the Wardens did not forget a person who could hold the deep. She had walked into the Nine that morning a woman whose entire craft was making things a little less than they were so no one would look, and she was walking out with the un-broken heart of the world in her hand and no idea at all what she was going to do with it.

lines.speaker: Iven Sarraz
lines.text: "So,"

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: Iven said, hoarse, propped on Brick's arm.

lines.speaker: Iven Sarraz
lines.text: "We certify it empty and safe, do we? Collect our double fee?"

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: Despite everything, Cael laughed — a short, cracked, astonished sound, the first honest noise she'd made in front of them in six years.

lines.speaker: Cael Ferren
lines.text: "No,"

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: she said. She unwrapped the fork, and looked at it, ugly and grey and true, and did not put it away.

lines.speaker: Cael Ferren
lines.text: "No, I don't think we do."

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: Behind them the Nine sat in the falling dark, empty now, and quiet, and — for the first turn in nine years — not looping at all. Ahead of them the lumen-lamps of Threnn came up one by one along the Nine Road, cold and blue and blind, listening, every one of them, to a note that had just walked out through the door and started for home.
